A proposed approach to material and historical evidence

Its minerals can help identify the material. Marks may help us ask how it was worked. Its location and surroundings can help us place it in a history.

Try those three views. The drawing is not a measured sample. It introduces a research approach that uses the pyramids to connect materials, making, preservation and historical evidence.

Choose a view of the stone. Each asks for a different kind of evidence.

Words used here
provenance
Where something came from and the history of how it reached us.
Read the fuller explanation

A stone in a monument is material, worked object and surviving record. Mineral assemblage, fracture, abrasion, transport, assembly and exposure constrain different parts of its history. None of those views is sufficient simply because it is detailed.

The material-history programme uses the pyramids as its named entry. It asks what sequences of selection, working, movement and preservation could leave the observed traces. Its register proposes research joins; it does not settle a monument’s history by drawing an attractive physical analogy.

The stone here is an illustration, not a measured sample. Move among its lenses: composition, working and context. Notice the different evidence each would need. A good question can cross scales without pretending to calculate an entire pyramid from first principles.
